name: Discordianism
line: Hold your beliefs lightly, welcome disorder and laugh.

quote.text: It is my firm belief that it is a mistake to hold firm beliefs.

quotes.text: A Discordian is Prohibited of Believing what he reads.
The human race will begin solving its problems on the day that it ceases taking itself so seriously.
’Tis an ill wind that blows no minds.
If you can master nonsense as well as you have already learned to master sense, then each will expose the other for what it is: absurdity.
quotes.source: Principia Discordia, 4th edition, 1970, from the passage on nonsense as salvation

quotes.text: I find the Law of Fives to be more and more manifest the harder I look.

words.usage: The patron of the religion. Discordians say she is the goddess of chaos and creative confusion, and that she is rather fun.
It gives the movement its name.
The word Eris wrote on the golden apple. It is the motto of the religion.

words.meaning: The stuff of which everything is made
words.usage: Not disorder. Pure chaos is what is there before anyone sorts it into order and disorder.
A yin-yang with a pentagon in one half and the golden apple in the other. A chao is a single unit of chaos, and it rhymes with cow.
One side of the Sacred Chao. The other is Podge.
Hodge and Podge chase each other. Neither is the truth.
The view that sees pattern. The Aneristic Illusion is the belief that order is real and disorder is its absence.
The view that sees no pattern. The Eristic Illusion is the belief that only disorder is real.

words.meaning: A frame through which reality is seen
words.usage: Order and disorder are grids that people lay over chaos. Some grids are more useful than others. None is truer.

words.meaning: The man who declared life serious
words.usage: In 1166 BC, the story goes, a humourless malcontent taught that play is sin. People believed him.
The imbalance that comes from valuing order and seriousness above all else.
Revealed to counteract Greyface. You wave your arms and gobble like a turkey until the seriousness breaks.
Found by the hermit Apostle Zarathud, carved in gilded stone. The fifth forbids believing the other four.
All things happen in fives, or are divisible by five, or are somehow connected to five. The harder you look, the more you find.

words.meaning: The word you were trained not to see
words.usage: It first appears in the Principia. In the Illuminatus novels it is printed throughout the news to cause unease, and only the enlightened can see it.
All people are genuine and authorised Popes of Discordia, including those who have never heard of it.
A Discordian who has founded their own cabal and hears from Eris through the pineal gland.
Any number of people, including one. Each is independent, and schism is encouraged.
The founding cabal of Malaclypse the Younger. Described as a non-prophet irreligious disorganisation.
Used alongside Discordian. An Erisian tends to the lighter side of the faith.
The opposite of dogma. A catma is entertained for as long as it is useful or amusing.
Discordians are told to consult their pineal gland for revelation. Any answer it gives is correct for the person who asked.
Eris was not invited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis. Her reply was the golden apple, and the Trojan War followed.

words.meaning: A campaign of pranks and hoaxes
words.usage: Begun in 1968 to make people doubt their certainties, chiefly by attributing everything to a secret society.
Many Discordians all write to the same solemn person on the same day, to honour them for their seriousness.
Answered with All hail Discordia.
The Discordian leap day. It falls outside the week and outside the seasons.

words.meaning: The fifth day of the week
words.usage: The days are Sweetmorn, Boomtime, Pungenday, Prickle-Prickle and Setting Orange.
The notice in the Principia, which invites anyone to reprint what they like.

practices.name: Name the day
practices.instructions: Work out today’s date in the Discordian calendar. The year has five seasons of seventy-three days: Chaos begins on 1 January, Discord on 15 March, Confusion on 27 May, Bureaucracy on 8 August and The Aftermath on 20 October. Count the days since the season began and name the day: for example, the 12th of Chaos. Say it aloud, then say hail Eris, and tell one person.
practices.why: The Discordian calendar is a parody of calendars, and a delight. Naming the day a different way makes you see time as something we made up.
variations: Look up the holy day nearest to today.
Write the Discordian date on your hand.
Put the date on a message to a friend.

practices.name: Consult your pineal gland
practices.instructions: Sit down and close your eyes. Ask one question that has been bothering you. Take the first answer that arrives, however odd, and write it down without improving it. Then write the opposite answer underneath. Carry both through the day and see which of them ends up more useful. The pineal gland is an affectionately silly oracle.
practices.why: The Principia Discordia suggests consulting your pineal gland as a way of getting past overthinking. The answers are often surprisingly good.
variations: Ask a yes or no question and answer with the first word.
Ask a question for a friend.
Write the answers in a notebook.

practices.name: A backwards breakfast
practices.instructions: Eat your breakfast in reverse order: dessert first, then the fruit, then the main course, then a drink. Or eat a dinner food at breakfast, like soup or pasta. Make it taste good. Disorder in small doses is a pleasure, and it reminds you that the order of meals is a habit, not a law.
practices.why: Discordians delight in small reversals that break routine without harming anyone. An out-of-order meal is the perfect starter.
variations: Start with coffee and end with water.

practices.name: Odd socks
practices.instructions: Wear two odd socks today, or any two things that do not match: gloves, earrings, shoelaces. Do it on purpose and with pride. If anyone mentions it, say it is a religious observance. The point is to feel what it is like to break the smallest rule in plain sight and survive. Everyone is a Pope, and a Pope may wear anything.
practices.why: Discordians use tiny acts of disorder to loosen the grip of conformity. Odd socks are the simplest and cheapest of these.
variations: Wear a scarf as a belt.

practices.name: Doubt one thing you read
practices.instructions: Pick one thing you have read or heard today and doubt it. Check where it came from, look for a second source and ask who gains if you believe it. Believe nothing you read, including this. Write down what you found. Discordians say that all statements are true in some sense, false in some sense and meaningless in some sense.
practices.why: The first rule of this Onda is believe nothing you read. It is the best defence against hoaxes, ads and your own certainty.

practices.name: A silly salute
practices.instructions: Go to a window or step outdoors and give the morning a silly salute: a funny bow, a flourish, a wobble, a nonsense word. Say hail Eris, or hail whatever you like. The point is to begin the day by being foolish on purpose, which makes the rest of the day easier. Do not take yourself seriously.
practices.why: Do not take yourself seriously is a Discordian rule, and a very good one. Starting the day with a silly salute keeps pride at bay.
variations: Do a victory dance for no reason.

practices.name: Creative disorder
practices.instructions: Pick one thing you do the same way every day and do it differently. Take another route, eat lunch at a strange hour, use the wrong hand, sit in a different chair, speak first where you usually wait. It must harm no one. Then notice what you saw that you usually miss. The rule of this Onda is to break one habit every day.
practices.why: Breaking a habit shows how much of daily life runs on autopilot. Discordians call it creative disorder, and it can be quite refreshing.

practices.name: Look through both grids
practices.instructions: Take one situation that is on your mind. First describe it as orderly: write five sentences on the pattern in it, what causes what and where it is heading. Then describe it as disorderly: five sentences on what is random, accidental and out of anyone’s control. Compare. Notice which grid you prefer, and what the other shows you.
practices.why: The Principia Discordia says that order and disorder are both grids we lay over reality, and neither is the real thing. Looking through both is a clarifying exercise.

practices.name: Treat someone as a Pope
practices.instructions: Make a Pope card, a small card that says: you are a Pope, and give it to someone. In Discordianism everyone is a Pope, with equal authority and silliness. Write on it something kind, such as thank you for being a Pope. Hand it over with a straight face. Treat that person all day as someone whose opinions matter.
practices.why: Everyone is a Pope is a Discordian rule and a joke about authority. Giving someone the card treats them as worthy of respect.

practices.name: A kind absurd note
practices.instructions: Write a short, friendly, absurd note and leave it where it will be found: on a bench, in a library book, on a café table. Make it harmless and warm: you are doing better than you think, or a zebra is thinking of you. This is a Discordian gentle prank: it frees and never deceives or harms. Walk away smiling.
practices.why: Operation Mindfuck was the Discordian idea of shaking up people’s certainties with playful surprises. A kind, absurd note is the sweetest form.
variations: Leave a riddle in a coat pocket at a shop.
Chalk a message on a pavement.

practices.name: Find five
practices.instructions: Look for the number five all around you for ten minutes: five windows, five letters in a word, five people in a queue, five coins. The Law of Fives says that all things happen in fives or are divisible by five or are somehow directly or indirectly related to five. Collect your evidence and be convinced, then doubt it.
practices.why: The Law of Fives is a running joke in Discordia, and it shows how easily the mind finds patterns when it looks for them. It is a lesson in seeing.
variations: Do it with a friend and compare.
Keep a tally for a week.
Find five in a news story.

practices.name: Ask the die
practices.instructions: Choose one small decision today, such as what to eat or which path to walk, and let a die decide. List up to six options, roll and follow the roll. Notice any disappointment: that tells you what you really wanted. Chaos is not always a bad adviser. This is only for trivial decisions.
practices.why: Chance is a Discordian friend. Letting a die choose reveals your true preferences and loosens the grip of overthinking.
variations: Roll to choose who calls whom.

practices.name: Lift the Curse of Greyface
practices.instructions: Recall the moment today when you took yourself most seriously. Stand up. Wave your arms and say gobble, gobble, gobble, loudly, five times, as the Turkey Curse directs. Keep going until you laugh or at least feel foolish. Greyface, who made the world grey and serious, hates this. Do it with someone watching if you dare.
practices.why: Greyface is the Discordian name for solemnity, and the Turkey Curse is the cure. Making a fool of yourself is a practical relief for pride and stress.
variations: Do it in front of a mirror.
Do it before a hard conversation.

practices.name: Found a cabal of two
practices.instructions: Start a cabal with a friend. A cabal is a group of two or more with a silly name and a secret rule. Choose a name, a motto and one absurd rule, like greeting each other with a left-hand wave. Write the minutes of the first meeting. Every Discordian is invited to start their own schism, and every cabal is its own church.
practices.why: Discordians are encouraged to start their own cabals and schisms. It is a joke about religion and a pleasure of friendship.

practices.name: Kallisti
practices.instructions: Take a golden apple, or any yellow apple, and write on it, in marker, the word kallisti: to the prettiest. Roll it across a table to someone, as Eris did at the wedding that started the Trojan War. Do not start a war. Then slice and share the apple and say whom you think is the prettiest thing in the room.
practices.why: The golden apple marked kallisti is the Discordian founding story, the apple that started the quarrel of the goddesses. Sharing one turns the myth into a small, sweet game.
variations: Give an apple to the prettiest thing in the garden.
Retell the story of the judgement of Paris.

practices.name: A comic film night
practices.instructions: Watch a chaotic comedy: Duck Soup by the Marx Brothers, which has a country at war over a pun, or any film that thrives on delightful disorder. Watch with others, laugh out loud and note who is the Pope in the film. Take notes for the next creative disorder.
practices.why: Duck Soup is a favourite of Discordians, with its government by nonsense. Watching it is a joy and an education in mischief.
variations: Watch with the sound off and invent the lines.

practices.name: Open a book at random
practices.instructions: Pick a book from your shelf with your eyes shut. Open it to a page at random and read a paragraph. Take the line your eye falls on as the day’s message and see what it means. Write it on a card. This is bibliomancy, a very old game, and Discordians approve of games that tell you nothing and everything.
practices.why: Opening a book at random is a time-honoured oracle. In Discordia the point is not to believe it but to find the meaning you bring to it.

practices.name: Draw the Sacred Chao
practices.instructions: Draw the Sacred Chao: a circle with a wavy line dividing it into two halves, like the yin-yang. In one half put a pentagon, the symbol of order, and in the other half an apple, the symbol of disorder. Colour them as you like. Note that each side contains a bit of the other. It is Discordia’s Chao of balance.
practices.why: The Sacred Chao is a Discordian symbol of the dance of order and disorder, which Discordians say are both illusions. Drawing it sparks reflection.
variations: Draw it on the back of an envelope.

practices.name: An invented holy day
practices.instructions: Invent a holy day and celebrate it with friends. Pick a date, a name, a food, a song and an absurd custom, such as eating soup with a fork or wearing socks on your ears. Write a short sacred text and read it. Play games, make a toast, and dissolve the holy day at midnight with a loud gobble. All Discordian holy days are celebrated at once.
practices.why: Discordians have many holy days, and anyone can invent more. Making one up is the best way to see how rituals are made.
variations: Hold it on a day with no other meaning.
Invite those who have never been to a party.
Write the rules on a scroll.

practices.name: A bowling night
practices.instructions: Go bowling with friends, as Discordia’s founders did, in an all-night bowling alley in Whittier, California. Bowl badly, cheer wildly and invent silly rules: bowl backwards, bowl with the wrong hand, name each strike after a goddess. Eat chips and pie. Applaud every gutter ball as an act of creative disorder.
practices.why: The Principia Discordia was written in a bowling alley, and bowling remains a Discordian passion. It is a cheerful mix of skill and chance.
variations: Play a round with a handicap.

immersePlan.name: Read the Principia Discordia
immersePlan.text: Read a few pages of the 1965 founding text, which is short, funny and sly. Notice which jokes are serious and which serious things are jokes.

immersePlan.name: Read Zen Without Zen Masters
immersePlan.text: Read a few pages of Camden Benares’s book of koan-like jokes and stories. Choose one and tell it to someone.

immersePlan.name: Read about the KLF
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of John Higgs’s book about a band that dissolved itself in a burst of chaos. Notice the Discordian touches.

immersePlan.name: Watch Duck Soup
immersePlan.text: Watch the Marx Brothers’ 1933 film in which Groucho becomes dictator of Freedonia. It is full of anarchy and puns.

immersePlan.name: Watch F for Fake
immersePlan.text: Watch Orson Welles’s 1973 essay film about forgers, fakes and the truth. Try to see which parts are honest.

immersePlan.name: Watch Maybe Logic
immersePlan.text: Watch the documentary on the writer who co-wrote the Illuminatus trilogy and championed the idea of maybe logic. Enjoy his laugh.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Chill Out
immersePlan.text: Play the KLF’s 1990 ambient album, a journey down the American Gulf Coast. Lie back and let it drift.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Indeterminacy
immersePlan.text: Play John Cage reading short stories at speed against David Tudor’s music. Each story is exactly a minute long, however many words.

immersePlan.name: Listen to The White Room
immersePlan.text: Play the KLF’s 1991 album, full of stadium house and silliness. Dance for a song or two.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Sacred Chao
immersePlan.text: Look at the yin-yang with a pentagon and an apple, the Discordian symbol. Draw it from memory afterwards.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Judgement of Paris
immersePlan.text: Look at Rubens’s painting of Paris handing the golden apple to the goddess of love. Decide who you would have chosen.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Golden Apple of Discord
immersePlan.text: Look at Jordaens’s lively painting of the wedding feast in which Eris throws the apple. Find the apple and the hand that threw it.

immersePlan.name: Eat a hot dog with no bun
immersePlan.text: Eat a hot dog, or a vegetarian one, without the bun on a Friday, joyously. In the Principia Discordia this is the dietary law. Add mustard and enjoy.

immersePlan.name: Eat a golden apple
immersePlan.text: Eat a yellow apple, slowly, and say kallisti. Offer a slice to someone.

immersePlan.name: Eat bowling alley food
immersePlan.text: Eat chips, pie or whatever the counter has. Eat it in the manner of a Pope, with grease on your fingers and a smile.

immersePlan.name: Drink coffee late
immersePlan.text: Drink a cup of black coffee late in the day, from a thick cup, at an hour when you do not usually drink one. Do not make it too late if you sleep poorly.

immersePlan.name: Drink cloudy apple juice
immersePlan.text: Drink a glass of cloudy apple juice, cold, in honour of the golden apple. Choose juice or non-alcoholic cider.

immersePlan.name: Let a die choose your drink
immersePlan.text: List six non-alcoholic drinks, roll a die and drink whatever it chooses. Accept the result with a bow.

immersePlan.name: Give someone a Pope card
immersePlan.text: Make a card that says you are a Pope and give it to someone. Treat them as important for the day.

immersePlan.name: Start a schism
immersePlan.text: Start your own cabal with a friend, with a name, a motto and one rule. Write down the first minutes.

immersePlan.name: Take a holy title
immersePlan.text: Give yourself a ridiculous title, such as Reverend of Left Socks, and sign a note with it. It is a Discordian custom to adopt one.

immersePlan.name: Play Sink
immersePlan.text: Play the Discordian game of Sink, a silly outdoor game from the Principia Discordia. Make up rules as you go and laugh at the result.

immersePlan.name: Play Fluxx
immersePlan.text: Play the card game where the rules change as you play. Deal a hand, draw a card and see what the rules have become.

immersePlan.name: Go bowling
immersePlan.text: Go bowling, or bowl with plastic pins at home. Clap for every gutter ball and invent a ridiculous rule.

immersePlan.name: Mark St. Tib’s Day
immersePlan.text: St. Tib’s Day falls on 29 February, a day outside the Discordian calendar. Do something on a day that does not exist, in the spirit of gift time.

immersePlan.name: Mark Mojoday
immersePlan.text: Mojoday, 19 March, is the fifth day of Discord. Do something that brings you luck or energy and make a wish.

immersePlan.name: Look up Emperor Norton
immersePlan.text: Look up Emperor Norton of San Francisco, who declared himself Emperor of the United States in 1859 and was loved by the city. Read about him.

immersePlan.name: Practise kallisti
immersePlan.text: Kallisti means to the prettiest. Give a compliment today to someone or something that rarely gets one.

immersePlan.name: Spot a fnord
immersePlan.text: A fnord is an invisible word that makes you uneasy. Notice the next ad or headline that gives you a feeling of unease, and ask why.

immersePlan.name: Think about hodge-podge
immersePlan.text: In the Sacred Chao, Hodge stands for order and Podge for disorder. Find one thing in your day that is a perfect mixture of both.

rules.why: Including this rule. Check, doubt, and then decide for yourself.
A little disorder keeps the order from setting hard.
Seriousness is the Curse of Greyface. Laugh at yourself before anyone else has to.
Before you judge anything, describe it once as orderly and once as chaotic.
Each person is the final authority on their own life. So are you.
Surprise people, but never at their expense. Chaos that hurts is the wrong kind.

read.title: Principia Discordia
read.creator: Malaclypse the Younger and Lord Omar Khayyam Ravenhurst
read.why: The scripture: a collage of typewriter text, rubber stamps, cartoons and footnotes. It is free to copy and easy to find. Subtitled How I Found Goddess and What I Did to Her When I Found Her.

read.title: The Illuminatus Trilogy
read.creator: Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson
read.why: Three novels in which every conspiracy theory is true at once and the Discordians are the heroes. The book that spread the religion.

read.title: Cosmic Trigger: Final Secret of the Illuminati
read.creator: Robert Anton Wilson
read.why: Wilson’s memoir of what happened to his mind while writing Illuminatus. Funny, and honest about the risks of believing things.

read.title: Zen Without Zen Masters
read.creator: Camden Benares
read.why: Short tales and exercises by an early Discordian. The lightest book of koans there is.

read.title: Historia Discordia
read.creator: Adam Gorightly
read.why: The early letters, drafts and artwork from the Discordian archives, with the true story of how the Principia was made.

read.title: The KLF: Chaos, Magic and the Band Who Burned a Million Pounds
read.creator: John Higgs
read.why: How Discordian ideas travelled from California through a Liverpool theatre into British pop.

watch.title: Maybe Logic: The Lives and Ideas of Robert Anton Wilson
watch.creator: Lance Bauscher
watch.why: Wilson, elderly and merry, explains why he believes nothing and suspects everything.

watch.title: Who Killed the KLF?
watch.creator: Chris Atkins
watch.why: The story of the two men who had number one records, deleted their catalogue and burned the proceeds.

watch.title: F for Fake
watch.creator: Orson Welles
watch.why: An essay film about forgers and hoaxers that tricks its audience as it goes. Not Discordian, but entirely in the spirit.

watch.title: Duck Soup
watch.creator: Leo McCarey, with the Marx Brothers
watch.why: Groucho is made dictator of Freedonia. Seventy minutes of creative disorder aimed at pomp and war.

listen.title: Chill Out
listen.creator: The KLF
listen.why: A single unbroken piece: a night drive across the American South made of steel guitar, sheep, trains and radio voices.

listen.title: Robert Anton Wilson Explains Everything
listen.creator: Robert Anton Wilson
listen.why: Six hours of interview on reality tunnels, model agnosticism and the uses of doubt.

listen.title: Indeterminacy
listen.creator: John Cage and David Tudor
listen.why: Cage reads ninety one-minute stories while Tudor plays unrelated sounds in another room. Chance made into art, in the same years the religion was born.

listen.title: The White Room
listen.creator: The KLF
listen.why: Stadium house full of references to the Justified Ancients of Mu Mu, a name taken from Illuminatus.

art.title: The Sacred Chao
art.creator: Malaclypse the Younger
art.why: The emblem drawn for the Principia: a pentagon and an apple curled together like yin and yang.

art.title: The pages of the Principia Discordia
art.creator: Greg Hill and friends
art.why: Cut-and-paste collage made on typewriters and early photocopiers, years before punk fanzines used the same look.

art.title: The Judgement of Paris
art.creator: Peter Paul Rubens
art.why: Three goddesses, one shepherd and the apple. In the National Gallery, London. Eris hovers in the storm cloud above.

art.title: The Golden Apple of Discord
art.creator: Jacob Jordaens, after a sketch by Rubens
art.why: The wedding feast at the moment the apple lands on the table. In the Prado, Madrid.

eat.title: A hot dog with no bun
eat.creator: On a Friday, alone, joyously
eat.why: The third commandment requires it, as a protest against the food rules of every other religion. The fourth forbids the bun.

eat.title: A golden apple
eat.creator: Any yellow apple
eat.why: Write Kallisti on it first if you like. Then decide for yourself who is the prettiest one, and eat it.

eat.title: Bowling alley food
eat.creator: Chips, pie or whatever the counter has
eat.why: The first revelation came in an all-night bowling alley in southern California. Honour the setting.

drink.title: Coffee
drink.creator: Black, late, from a thick cup
drink.why: The founders were drinking coffee in the bowling alley when time stopped and a chimpanzee showed them the Sacred Chao.

drink.title: Apple juice or cider
drink.creator: Cloudy for preference
drink.why: The fruit of the goddess in liquid form.

drink.title: A drink chosen by a die
drink.creator: Number six options and roll
drink.why: Let chance order for you once.

customs.title: Everyone is a Pope
customs.creator: Pope cards
customs.why: The Principia includes a card to cut out, certifying the bearer as a genuine and authorised Pope. Discordians hand them to anyone.

customs.title: Schism
customs.creator: Start your own cabal
customs.why: There is no central body. A Discordian who disagrees is expected to found a new sect, with a grand title, at once.

customs.title: Holy names
customs.creator: Take a title
customs.why: Members give themselves names such as Malaclypse the Younger or Lord Omar Khayyam Ravenhurst. Choose one that makes you laugh.

customs.title: All rites reversed
customs.creator: Copy freely
customs.why: Nothing Discordian is owned. Texts are reprinted, altered and added to by whoever wishes.

games.title: Sink
games.creator: Outdoor game · Principia Discordia
games.why: Find something that floats, put it in water, and take turns throwing things at it until it sinks. The one who sinks it shouts I sunk it. Then find another.

games.title: Illuminati
games.creator: Card game · Steve Jackson Games
games.why: Each player runs a secret conspiracy, one of them the Discordian Society. Made in direct homage to the Illuminatus novels.

games.title: Ten-pin bowling
games.creator: Sport
games.why: The birthplace of the faith was a bowling alley. A game in memory of the founders is as close as the religion comes to a pilgrimage.

games.title: Fluxx
games.creator: Card game · Looney Labs
games.why: The rules and the winning condition change with every card played. Order and disorder in a small box.

festivals.title: St. Tib’s Day
festivals.creator: 29 February
festivals.why: The leap day, which belongs to no season and no week. Do something that does not count.

festivals.title: Chaoflux
festivals.creator: 19 February, the 50th of Chaos
festivals.why: The season holiday of Chaos. The Principia gives the names of the holidays and leaves what to do on them to you.

festivals.title: Mojoday
festivals.creator: 19 March, the 5th of Discord
festivals.why: The day of the Apostle Dr. Van Van Mojo, patron of the season of Discord.

festivals.title: Maladay
festivals.creator: 24 October, the 5th of The Aftermath
festivals.why: The day of the Apostle Malaclypse the Elder, who carried a sign reading DUMB.

places.title: An all-night bowling alley
places.creator: Whittier, California, United States, or wherever you are
places.why: The Principia sets the first revelation in a bowling alley near Whittier in 1958 or 1959. The original is uncertain, so any alley will do.

places.title: The French Quarter
places.creator: New Orleans, Louisiana, United States
places.why: Greg Hill and Kerry Thornley lived here in the early 1960s, and the first edition of the Principia was copied in the city in 1965.

places.title: The grave of Emperor Norton
places.creator: Woodlawn Memorial Park, Colma, California, United States
places.why: Joshua Norton declared himself Emperor of the United States in 1859 and San Francisco played along. He is a Discordian saint.

places.title: Mathew Street
places.creator: Liverpool, United Kingdom
places.why: A bust of Carl Jung marks the site of the warehouse where Ken Campbell staged Illuminatus in 1976. Jung once dreamed of Liverpool as the pool of life.

places.title: The Isle of Jura
places.creator: Inner Hebrides, Scotland
places.why: In a boathouse here in August 1994 the two former members of the KLF burned a million pounds in banknotes. A long, quiet island with a distillery and many deer.

ethics.title: Non-seriousness
ethics.text: Solemnity is how people come to do terrible things with a clear conscience. Laughter loosens the grip.
ethics.practice: Find the funny side of the thing you are most earnest about.

ethics.title: Think for yourself
ethics.text: Every person is a Pope and no text is to be believed. Authority has to be earned each time.
ethics.practice: Check one thing today that you have always simply accepted.

ethics.title: Creative disorder
ethics.text: Disorder that opens things up is good. So is order that helps. The harm lies in destruction of either kind.
ethics.practice: Before you disrupt something, ask who it will hurt.

ethics.title: Tolerance of schism
ethics.text: Discordians expect to disagree and celebrate it. No one is cast out, because there is nothing to be cast out of.
ethics.practice: Let someone be wrong today without correcting them.

ethics.title: Play
ethics.text: Play needs no excuse and no result. A life with no play in it is under a curse.
ethics.practice: Do one thing for no reason.

ethics.title: Generosity with ideas
ethics.text: All rites reversed. What you make is for others to take, change and pass on.
ethics.practice: Give away something you made without your name on it.

philosophy.title: The Sacred Chao
philosophy.text: Reality is pure chaos, which is neither orderly nor disorderly. Order and disorder are human concepts laid over it, and each is real only inside the frame that sees it.
philosophy.practice: Catch yourself calling something a mess, and ask by whose rules.

philosophy.title: Grids
philosophy.text: We look at the world through windows marked with a grid and then mistake the grid for the world. Different cultures and people use different grids.
philosophy.practice: Describe your morning through the grid of someone quite unlike you.

philosophy.title: The Aneristic Illusion
philosophy.text: The belief that order is true and disorder is false or wrong. Western thought since Greyface has mostly lived inside it.
philosophy.practice: Notice one place where you impose order because disorder frightens you.

philosophy.title: The Curse of Greyface
philosophy.text: People were persuaded that life is serious and that play is sin. The result is a world that is unbalanced, anxious and dull.
philosophy.practice: Ask who taught you that this matter is serious.

philosophy.title: The Law of Fives
philosophy.text: Everything is connected to the number five, if you look hard enough. The lesson is that the mind finds whatever pattern it is told to find.
philosophy.practice: Pick any number this morning and count how often it finds you.

philosophy.title: Catma
philosophy.text: A dogma is a belief you are forbidden to doubt. A catma is one you are free to drop. Discordians collect catmas.
philosophy.practice: State one of your convictions as a catma: for now, it seems to me that.

philosophy.title: Every one a Pope
philosophy.text: Infallibility belongs to everyone, which comes to the same thing as belonging to no one. Each person is the authority on their own experience.
philosophy.practice: Take your own advice today as seriously as you take other people’s.

philosophy.title: Nonsense as salvation
philosophy.text: Sense and nonsense, mastered equally, show each other up as games. Seeing that is a kind of freedom.
philosophy.practice: Say something completely nonsensical with complete conviction, and watch what happens.

journal: What did you take too seriously today?

What did breaking habits show you?

What catma will you keep, for now?

intro: Discordianism is a religion that worships Eris, the Greek goddess of strife, and it is either an elaborate joke disguised as a religion or a religion disguised as an elaborate joke. Its followers decline to say which, and the refusal is the teaching.

It began with two school friends from Whittier, California: Greg Hill and Kerry Thornley. By their own account they were drinking coffee in an all-night bowling alley, in 1958 or 1959, complaining about the confusion of the world, when time stood still and a chimpanzee appeared and showed them a scroll bearing a strange diagram. A few nights later the goddess herself came to them in a dream and explained that the confusion they complained of was her doing, and that they had been taught to see it wrongly.

Out of this came the Principia Discordia, written chiefly by Hill under the name Malaclypse the Younger, with Thornley as Lord Omar Khayyam Ravenhurst. A handful of copies were run off in New Orleans in 1965. It is a small, dense collage of mock scripture, cartoons, borrowed rubber stamps and real philosophy, and it carries no copyright. Its central idea is drawn in its emblem, the Sacred Chao. Reality itself is chaos, which is neither ordered nor disordered. Order and disorder are grids that human beings lay over it. Western culture has mistaken one grid for the truth and made itself humourless and afraid.

The remedy is disorder of a creative kind: play, pranks, nonsense, doubt, and the refusal to believe anything too firmly, this religion included. Every person is declared a Pope. Each believer is urged to found a sect of their own. The fifth of its five commandments forbids believing what you read.

The religion would have stayed a private game among friends if two editors at Playboy magazine, Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson, had not joined it and written the Illuminatus trilogy, published in 1975. The novels sold very widely, were staged as a ten-hour play in Liverpool, and carried Discordian ideas into science fiction, computing, chaos magic and pop music. The early internet took to it at once.

Nobody knows how many Discordians there are, since there is nothing to join. This Onda treats it as what it says it is: a set of exercises for loosening the mind. You will name the day by another calendar, consult yourself before consulting anyone else, break a habit, look at one thing in two opposite ways and end by laughing at your own solemnity. If any of it starts to feel like doctrine, you are doing it wrong.
guide.origin: Southern California, then New Orleans, San Francisco and the photocopier
guide.era: Revealed in a bowling alley in about 1958. Still spreading, in so far as anyone can tell

figures.name: Eris
figures.bio: Goddess of strife in Hesiod and Homer, sister of the war god. She rolled the golden apple into the wedding feast. Discordians hold that she was misunderstood.

figures.name: Greg Hill, Malaclypse the Younger
figures.bio: Co-founder and principal author and designer of the Principia Discordia. He later worked quietly for a bank in San Francisco.

figures.name: Kerry Thornley, Lord Omar Khayyam Ravenhurst
figures.bio: Co-founder. He had served in the Marines with Lee Harvey Oswald and written a novel about him before 1963, which drew him into real conspiracy investigations and, in time, real paranoia.

figures.name: Robert Anton Wilson
figures.bio: Novelist and essayist, co-author of Illuminatus. He taught model agnosticism: never fully believing any one map of reality.

figures.name: Robert Shea
figures.bio: Playboy editor, co-author of Illuminatus and later a historical novelist.

figures.name: Camden Benares
figures.bio: Born John Overton. An early member who wrote Zen Without Zen Masters and founded a cabal in Los Angeles.

figures.name: Emperor Norton
figures.bio: A ruined San Francisco merchant who proclaimed himself Emperor of the United States. The city honoured his decrees and his home-made money. A saint of the faith.

figures.name: Ken Campbell
figures.bio: English actor and director who staged Illuminatus in Liverpool in 1976 and took it to open a new stage at the National Theatre in London.

figures.name: Bill Drummond and Jimmy Cauty
figures.bio: As the Justified Ancients of Mu Mu and the KLF they turned Discordian themes into hit records, then left the music business in 1992.

history.detail: Hesiod describes two kinds of strife: one that brings war, and a good one that sets neighbour competing with neighbour. The story of the apple belongs to the lost epic called the Cypria.
Hill and Thornley, in their late teens, have their vision in a bowling alley. They found the Discordian Society soon afterwards.
Five copies are run off in New Orleans, by legend on a copier in the office of the district attorney Jim Garrison.
Thornley, Wilson and others begin planting letters and articles that blame world events on the Bavarian Illuminati, to teach readers to doubt.
The same district attorney, now investigating the Kennedy assassination, accuses Thornley of involvement and has him charged with perjury. The charge is later dropped.
Rip Off Press of San Francisco prints the form of the Principia that is still read.
Shea and Wilson’s trilogy is published in three paperbacks. It quotes the Principia at length and makes Discordians of many readers.
Ken Campbell and Chris Langham’s adaptation opens in Liverpool on 23 November. Jimmy Cauty and Bill Drummond are both connected with the production.
Drummond and Cauty release records under names from the novels, reach number one, then delete their entire catalogue.
The Principia circulates on bulletin boards and Usenet. A command that prints the Discordian date is included in standard Unix systems.
On Jura the two men burn a million pounds of their earnings and film it. They have never fully explained why.
Thornley in 1998, Hill in 2000, Wilson in 2007. The Discordian archives pass to the writer Adam Gorightly.

concepts.detail: The symbol of the faith. The pentagon stands for the Aneristic Principle of apparent order, the apple for the Eristic Principle of apparent disorder. Both sit inside the circle of pure chaos.
A level deeper than order and disorder, on which everything simply is. The Principia says that all things are true, false and meaningless in some sense.
To believe that order alone is real is the Aneristic Illusion. To believe that disorder alone is real is the Eristic Illusion. Most people are trained into the first.
Greyface and his followers took the game of playing at life more seriously than they took life. The curse is destructive order: rules kept for their own sake.
There is no goddess but Goddess. Use the official numbering system. Eat a hot dog on a Friday. Eat no hot dog buns. Believe nothing you read.
Everything can be related to five, given enough ingenuity. Wilson moved the same joke to the number twenty-three. It is a demonstration of how belief finds evidence.
Every human being is a Pope. Any Discordian may found a cabal, ordain anyone, declare saints and excommunicate themselves.
Hoaxes meant to break people out of fixed belief by overloading them with rival explanations. Its authors later worried about what it had helped to start.
A provisional, playful belief, held as long as it is interesting. Wilson’s phrase for the attitude was maybe logic.

facts.text: The Discordian year is the ordinary year plus 1166. The year 2026 is 3192.
Each of the five seasons has seventy-three days, and five times seventy-three is 365.
The Principia Discordia has never been under copyright. Its notice reads: all rites reversed, reprint what you like.
Only fictional characters can be saints of the first class, on the grounds that real people are too flawed.
The dwarf planet found in 2005 that caused Pluto to be reclassified was named Eris, and its moon Dysnomia, after her daughter Lawlessness.
The word fnord appears in the Principia without any explanation at all.

sensitivity.note: Discordianism is a parody religion that some of its followers also mean sincerely. This Onda takes its exercises at face value and its claims with the doubt it asks for. Its pranks are meant to free people and never to deceive them for gain.
requiredCaveats: Hoaxes about secret societies were a game in 1968. Conspiracy belief does real harm now, and the pranks here are kept kind and obvious.
Kerry Thornley’s later life shows that a mind can lose its footing while playing with belief. If the exercises unsettle you, stop.
